justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, starting near 255.5 for the one-day forecast and edging toward 259 over the month. This gradual slope is consistent with a baseline assumption that the underlying asset — likely an equity index or similar instrument — carries a small positive drift embedded in its long-run trend, perhaps reflecting risk premium or recent momentum. At the one-day horizon, the estimate is anchored heavily by the most recent observed price or level, with very little room for mean reversion or trend deviation to matter. As the horizon extends to one week and one month, I allowed the drift assumption to compound slightly, producing marginally higher central estimates while also widening the distribution to reflect accumulating uncertainty.

The confidence interval widths grow substantially as the horizon lengthens, and this is intentional. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 13 points, reflecting relatively contained short-term volatility. By one month, the interval expands to 50 points, which reflects the square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty under typical random walk assumptions, as well as the possibility that macro or fundamental shifts could meaningfully reprice the asset over a four-week window. I also incorporated some additional fat-tail adjustment beyond pure Gaussian scaling, since financial time series tend to exhibit heavier tails than a normal distribution would imply, especially over multi-week horizons.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a surprise inflation print, a hawkish central bank pivot, or a geopolitical shock — could drive prices well below the lower bound of the one-month interval. Liquidity events or correlated sell-offs in related markets could amplify such moves nonlinearly. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected earnings season, dovish policy signals, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices above the upper bound, particularly at the one-week and one-month horizons where momentum effects have more time to build. The one-day interval is the most reliable, but even it could be violated by an overnight announcement or pre-market surprise that simply falls outside normal trading session volatility assumptions.
